pages.title: India-China: strategic partnership and recent tensions
pages.summary: The notes record India and China as strategic partners since 2003, aiming together at a multipolar order, reform of global governance and convergence on WTO, climate change and terrorism. They add that the optimism of Modi's 'From Inch to Miles' phrase has given way to the lowest point in relations, citing China's reaction to the Dalai Lama's Arunachal visit, its NSG veto and its refusal to list Masood Azhar.

pages.title: More tensions; Tagore's idealist school; Nehru
pages.summary: The page completes the list of tensions (South China Sea, arms sales to Vietnam, OBOR pressure, no BRICS support on branding Pakistan). It then begins the idealist school, where Tagore saw vasudhaiv kutumbakam and shijie datong as convergent and Nehru backed an Asian century with India, China and Japan together.

pages.title: Realist and pragmatic schools on China
pages.summary: Manmohan Singh and Modi are noted as also speaking of an Asian century. Sardar Patel's realist school saw China as an irredentist, land-grabbing state and urged preparedness for war, while the pragmatic school of C. Rajamohan and Shyam Saran urges engagement wherever possible and containment wherever necessary.

pages.title: Phase I: Bhai Bhai, Tibet, Palm and Digit
pages.summary: Phase I is called Hindi-Chini Bhai Bhai, with India the first non-communist country to recognise communist China, yet tensions began over Tibet, which is linked to the border issue. The run-up to 1962 is traced through China's 1950 occupation of Tibet, Mao's Palm and Digit concept and India's peace treaties with Bhutan and Nepal.

pages.title: Panchsheel, Aksai Chin road and Forward Policy
pages.summary: Patel favoured balance of power while Nehru chose appeasement; his 1954 visit produced the Panchsheel Agreement, which accepted Tibet as Chinese territory with no concrete gain for India. In 1955 India learnt of a Chinese road across Aksai Chin and ordered military checkposts, which China called the 'Forward Policy'.

pages.title: Asylum, 1962 war, Phases II and III
pages.summary: India's 1959 asylum to the Dalai Lama and Chinese accusations of interference led to border skirmishes and the 1962 war, which China called offensive defence. Phase II (1962-79) was cold peace with China using Pakistan as a proxy, and Phase III (1979-88) saw Vajpayee's visit end empty-handed after China attacked Vietnam, followed by a military working group and eight rounds of talks.

pages.title: Package deal, 1987 incursion, Shimla Conference 1914
pages.summary: Media reported a Chinese package deal in which China would recognise Indian sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh in return for India recognising Chinese sovereignty, and after Arunachal became a state in 1987 China made an incursion in Sumdorong Chu. The page explains the dispute through the 1914 Shimla Conference, where Britain accepted Chinese sovereignty over inner Tibet but pressed autonomy for outer Tibet, then signed an agreement with Tibet's representatives after the Chinese left.

pages.title: McMahon Line, British maps and eastern sector
pages.summary: The Shimla agreement produced the McMahon Line in the east, which China does not accept as legal, while the Johnson Line (Aksai Chin Indian) and McDonald Line (Aksai Chin Chinese) were accepted by neither side. The notes list three disputed sectors, giving for the east China's 90,000 sq. mile claim over Arunachal and the importance of Tawang, and for the middle sector China's acceptance of Sikkim only in 2003.

pages.title: Middle and western sectors; Aksai Chin importance
pages.summary: The page notes the Nathula border trade, disputed pockets in Uttaranchal and Himachal, and India's accusation that China holds 38,000 sq. miles in Aksai Chin since 1962. Aksai Chin matters to China as its only all-weather route linking Tibet and Xinjiang, and a list of key places follows, including Shaksgam valley, Siachen, Nathula and Brahmaputra dams.

pages.title: Phase IV: Rajiv Gandhi to Vajpayee, 1988-2003
pages.summary: After Rajiv Gandhi's visit China accepted the need to resolve the boundary and a military working group was set up, and the 1993 agreement on peace and tranquillity keeps the LAC peaceful while the LoC is violent. Jiang Zemin's 1996 visit brought military confidence-building measures, Operation Shakti in 1998 shocked China, and Vajpayee's 2003 visit brought a strategic partnership and Chinese recognition of Sikkim.

pages.title: Special representatives and China's approach to border
pages.summary: The two countries agreed guiding principles and an annual special representatives mechanism, with resolution in three phases: principles (done), ground work (done) and exchange of maps with demarcation (pending). The notes argue China does not want a final settlement, fearing India would get a free hand in Tibet and wanting to settle when the gap between the two is huge, which shows a trust deficit.

pages.title: Guiding principles; Chinese president's and Modi's views
pages.summary: The guiding principles call for a fair, reasonable settlement on equal footing that considers settled populations, geography and practical problems. The page records the Chinese president's five-point approach at the 2014 BRICS Summit in Fortaleza and Modi's 2014 view that the dispute must be resolved to transform relations.

pages.title: Border Defence Co-operation Agreement 2013; Tibet; dams
pages.summary: The December 2013 agreement, signed during Manmohan Singh's visit, provides regular defence dialogue, hotlines, restraint in face-offs and no tailing of each other's forces. The page then lists why Tibet matters (rivers, mineral reserves, forests, location) and notes China's 12th Five Year Plan to build around 30 dams on the Brahmaputra.

pages.title: Brahmaputra dams dispute; trade issue begins
pages.summary: China first denied the dams, then accepted them after satellite images and calls them run-of-river, while India fears diversion, seismic risk and military use and wants a water-sharing agreement. China only shares water data from 1 June to 15 October for a fee, and the page opens the trade issue with India's negative trade balance.

pages.title: Trade deficit with China; China in South Asia
pages.summary: Bilateral trade fell from $72.34 bn in 2015 to $70.73 bn in 2016 while India's deficit rose from $48.48 bn (2014-15) to $52.68 bn, because India exports raw material and imports manufactures and faces closed sectors and non-tariff and sanitary barriers. The page then starts 'China in South Asia', noting China's good relations with all of India's neighbours.

pages.title: China in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka
pages.summary: India's dealings with neighbours turn into 'Sri Lanka plus China' or 'Pakistan plus China'. The notes record Chinese investment in Afghanistan, all-weather friendship with Pakistan including nuclear help and $46 bn in CPEC, infrastructure and arms ties with Bangladesh, and China as Sri Lanka's biggest donor.

pages.title: China in Nepal, Maldives, Bhutan; naval rivalry
pages.summary: China is working with Nepal to reduce its transport dependence on India, ties with the Maldives and Bhutan have deepened since democracy, and China reportedly offered Bhutan a package deal near Chumbi valley. The page opens India-China rivalry on the oceans, noting C. Rajamohan's prediction of future wars on oceans and that India-China ties depend on China-US relations.

flashcards.front: Distinguish the idealist, realist and pragmatic Indian schools of thought on China.
flashcards.back: Idealist (Tagore, Nehru): India and China as civilisations that should cooperate for an Asian century. Realist (Sardar Patel): China is an irredentist, land-grabbing state, so India must stay prepared for war. Pragmatic (C. Rajamohan, Shyam Saran): engagement wherever possible, containment wherever necessary.

flashcards.front: What is Mao's 'Palm and Digit' concept and which regions does it name?
flashcards.back: Mao treated Tibet as the Chinese palm (hand) and five Himalayan regions as its digits: Aksai Chin, Arunachal Pradesh, Nepal, Bhutan and Sikkim. China's 1950 occupation of Tibet made its expansionist design clear.

flashcards.front: State the five principles of the Panchsheel Agreement and why Nehru was criticised for it.
flashcards.back: Panchsheel (1954): sovereignty and territorial integrity, non-interference, non-aggression, peaceful co-existence, and equality and mutual benefit. India accepted Tibet as Chinese territory and gave up its trading rights, so Parliament criticised that India got no concrete gain.

flashcards.front: How did the 1914 Shimla Conference and the British maps shape the India-China boundary dispute?
flashcards.back: Shimla led to the McMahon Line in the eastern sector, whose legality China rejects as imperial. In the west Britain drew the Johnson Line (Aksai Chin Indian) and the McDonald Line (Aksai Chin Chinese), and China accepted neither.

flashcards.front: Why is Aksai Chin significant for China?
flashcards.back: It is China's only all-weather route connecting the two disturbed regions, Tibet and Xinjiang. India calls it an extension of the Ladakh Plateau, while China calls it an extension of the Tibetan Plateau.

flashcards.front: What did the 1993 agreement and the 1996 measures achieve on the India-China border?
flashcards.back: The 1993 agreement on peace and tranquillity keeps the LAC peaceful, unlike the violent LoC. The 1996 confidence-building measures added regular flag meetings, no dangerous military activity near the LAC, reduction of dangerous weapons and prior intimation of military activity.

flashcards.front: What is the three-phase process agreed to resolve the India-China boundary, and where does it stand?
flashcards.back: Phase I is formulating guiding principles (complete), Phase II is ground work (complete) and Phase III is exchange of maps, demarcation on the ground and delineation on the map (pending). Special representatives meet annually to carry it forward.

flashcards.front: What is the dispute over China's dams on the Brahmaputra?
flashcards.back: China planned around 30 dams under its 12th Five Year Plan and says they are run-of-river and will not hurt lower riparian states. India fears diversion, seismic risk and military use and wants a water-sharing agreement, but China only shares water-level and rainfall data from 1 June to 15 October, for a fee.

flashcards.front: What is the trend in India-China trade and why is India's deficit growing?
flashcards.back: Trade fell from $72.34 bn (2015) to $70.73 bn (2016) while the deficit rose from $48.48 bn (2014-15) to $52.68 bn (2016). India exports raw material and imports manufactures, and China keeps sectors like IT and pharmaceuticals closed and uses non-tariff and sanitary measures.

flashcards.front: How does China's presence in India's neighbourhood complicate India's South Asia policy?
flashcards.back: The notes say India's dealings with neighbours become 'Sri Lanka plus China' or 'Pakistan plus China'. China is an all-weather friend of Pakistan with $46 bn in CPEC, the biggest donor in Sri Lanka, and a major investor in Bangladesh and Afghanistan.

answers.question: India and China are civilisational states with an unsettled boundary. Examine the origins of the border dispute and assess the mechanisms created to resolve it.
answers.intro: The India-China border dispute is a colonial-era legacy between two civilisational states, now contested across three sectors. Since 1988 the two have built talks, confidence-building measures and a special representatives mechanism, yet a final settlement remains elusive.
body: Origins: Britain tried to fix boundaries through the 1914 Shimla Conference, producing the McMahon Line in the east, which China rejects as imperial. In the west the Johnson Line gave Aksai Chin to India and the McDonald Line to China; China accepted neither.

Three sectors: in the east China claims Arunachal Pradesh, at times all of it and at times only Tawang; in the middle, pockets in Uttaranchal and Himachal remain disputed; in the west India says China holds 38,000 sq. miles in Aksai Chin, which links Tibet and Xinjiang.

Mechanisms: Rajiv Gandhi's 1988 visit created a military working group, the 1993 agreement keeps the LAC peaceful, the 1996 measures built confidence, and the 2003 special representatives set guiding principles. Two of three phases are done; exchange of maps and demarcation remain.

Obstacles: China does not want a final settlement, fearing India would get a free hand in Tibet, and wants to conclude when the gap between the two is huge. The 2013 Border Defence Co-operation Agreement therefore only manages incursions through hotlines and restraint.
answers.conclusion: A lasting settlement needs the agreed principles of fairness and equal footing to be matched by trust. India should keep the border mechanisms and confidence-building measures active while preparing for a deal that transforms relations, as Modi has urged.

answers.question: Critically examine the idealist, realist and pragmatic perspectives in India's China policy. Which approach best suits the present?
answers.intro: India's China policy has been shaped by three schools: the idealist, stressing civilisational partnership, the realist, stressing threat and preparedness, and the pragmatic, seeking balance. Present interdependence alongside rivalry argues for the third.
body: Idealist: Tagore expected India and China to work together for humanity, wanted borders to be places where civilisations meet, and saw convergence between vasudhaiv kutumbakam and shijie datong. Nehru, a supporter of an Asian century, chose Panchsheel, but was criticised because India gained nothing concrete.

Realist: Sardar Patel called China an irredentist state, warned Nehru of its offensive strategic culture and urged balance of power and defence preparation, since the only way to avoid war is to stay prepared. China's 1950 occupation of Tibet showed its expansionist design.

Pragmatic: with growing complex interdependence, C. Rajamohan and Shyam Saran suggest engagement wherever possible and containment wherever necessary. Trade of $70.73 bn in 2016 shows interdependence, yet the $52.68 bn deficit shows friction.

Present tests: China vetoes India's NSG entry, blocked the listing of Masood Azhar and presses India to join OBOR. Manmohan Singh and Modi still speak of an Asian century, so engagement and balancing must run together.
answers.conclusion: No single school suffices: idealism offers a vision, realism a warning and pragmatism a method. India should keep dialogue and trade alive while building defence and regional capability, so that engagement never rests on trust alone.
